analysis.one_liner: Bans application and screening fees, caps late fees, and requires full fee and cost disclosure for renters in federally backed housing.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 28 House Democrats, has sat without a vote since its June 2025 introduction, moving only to a subcommittee in December.
analysis.plain_summary: The End Junk Fees for Renters Act would prohibit landlords of units backed by federal mortgage programs — FHA, VA, USDA, and Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac loans — from charging renters application fees and tenant screening fees, and would cap late fees at under 3 percent of monthly rent, charged no sooner than 15 days after rent is due. It would also require landlords to disclose total monthly costs, past litigation with tenants, ongoing pest and maintenance problems, and ten years of rent increases before a lease is signed. It directs federal regulators to write the rules, and makes reporting unpaid junk fees to credit bureaus an unfair debt collection practice.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters in apartments and homes financed by federal mortgage programs. They would no longer pay to simply apply for housing or for the background check a landlord runs on them, and they would see the true monthly cost, the landlord's court history, and the building's condition before signing a lease. Renters behind on rent would get a longer grace period and a capped late fee, and unpaid junk fees could not be reported to credit bureaus.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits owners of covered rental units from charging any fee to a household submitting a rental application, and any fee for criminal history, tenant screening, or consumer report background checks [S2].
Caps late fees at less than 3 percent of monthly rent and requires at least 15 days to have elapsed after rent is due before a late fee can be imposed, with these terms disclosed in the lease [S2].

Requires landlords to disclose, before a lease is signed, the total monthly amount due including fees, any litigation history with tenants, ongoing pest and maintenance issues, and the property's rent increases over the past ten years [S2].

Directs the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the FTC to define rental 'junk fees' and to treat furnishing unpaid junk fee information to a consumer reporting agency as an unfair debt collection practice under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, protecting renters' credit scores [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Landlords of federally financed rental housing, who currently collect application and screening fees from applicants and charge late fees of their own choosing. The fees they lose from applicants and the capped late fees would come out of rental income, and small landlords would face new pre-lease disclosure requirements. Tenant screening companies and credit bureaus would lose the business of application-time background checks and the leverage of reporting junk fees to credit files.
analysis.who_pays_short: Landlords, tenant screening firms, credit bureaus

drawbacks.text: The costs are real but narrow: the rules apply only to units backed by federal mortgage programs — FHA, VA, USDA, or Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac loans — so renters in buildings financed entirely with private money get none of these protections [S2].
Landlords lose fee income and could absorb it by raising base rent or passing costs to tenants, which could partly offset the savings; the bill does not limit base rent increases [S2].

Small landlords would bear new paperwork: a mandatory pre-lease disclosure covering litigation history, maintenance issues, and a decade of rent increases, with no exemption for owners of one or two units [S2].

Capping late fees and delaying their start to 15 days could make some landlords less patient with late payment and could tighten screening on marginal applicants, since application and screening costs currently fall on applicants rather than the landlord [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For renters, the direct gains are clear and immediate: fees that can run into the hundreds of dollars per application, repeated across multiple applications during a housing search, disappear, and renters see the real cost and condition of a unit before signing. The main honest caveats are that the bill covers only federally financed housing, some costs could reappear in base rent, and small landlords face new disclosure burdens. On balance the protections for renters outweigh the compliance and income costs to landlords, but the limited coverage means most of the rental market would still be unregulated.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and the Veterans' Affairs Committee in June 2025, and in December was referred only to a Financial Services subcommittee, so it has not come up for any vote and remains stuck in committee [S4].

narrative.text: Representative Maxwell Frost introduced the End Junk Fees for Renters Act on June 24, 2025, with 27 Democratic cosponsors listed on the bill [S1][S2][S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services and, in addition, to the Committee on Veterans' Affairs on the day of introduction [S4].
Six months later, on December 19, 2025, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity, and no committee vote, hearing, or floor vote appears in the action history [S4].
All 27 cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican has signed on [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, landlords of federally financed housing and the tenant screening industry are better off: none of the fee bans, late fee caps, or disclosure rules have been enacted, and the bill has not advanced past subcommittee referral in the six months since introduction.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Landlords and screening companies, so far

for.name: Maxwell Frost
for.what_they_did: Introduced the End Junk Fees for Renters Act on June 24, 2025 [S2][S4].

for.name: 27 House Democrats
for.role: Original cosponsors, including Reps. Gomez, Chu, Casar, Khanna, Schakowsky, Tlaib, Ocasio-Cortez, Jayapal, and others
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; all 27 listed cosponsors are Democrats [S3].

sides.party_line_note: All 27 cosponsors are Democrats and no Republican sponsor appears, while the Republican-led House committee process has not scheduled any action on the bill [S3][S4].

industries.industry: Landlords of federally financed rental housing
industries.note: The bill eliminates application and screening fees these owners collect from applicants and caps late fees below 3 percent of rent with a 15-day grace period, plus new pre-lease disclosure duties. Their fee revenue and pricing flexibility come directly from renters' pockets.

industries.industry: Tenant screening and background check companies
industries.note: The bill bans landlords from charging applicants for criminal history, tenant screening, and consumer report checks, removing a fee stream that today is billed to renters, not landlords.

industries.industry: Credit bureaus and consumer reporting agencies
industries.note: The bill directs regulators to treat furnishing unpaid rental junk fees to a credit reporting agency as an unfair debt collection practice, cutting off a tool landlords currently use to pressure tenants by threatening their credit [S2].

industries.industry: Mortgage lenders and housing finance (FHA, VA, USDA, Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac)
industries.note: The bill builds its renter protections entirely on federal mortgage-backing structures, defining coverage by FHA, VA, USDA, and Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac loans rather than extending rights to all renters. Federal housing finance becomes the delivery channel, and renters outside it remain unprotected.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in a subcommittee with all-Democratic sponsorship in a Republican-controlled House, a pattern under which housing fee bills introduced in a first session rarely reach a floor vote. Unless it gains Republican cosponsors or a committee markup is scheduled in the second session, it is likely to die at the end of the 119th Congress without a vote.
